entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Involving strong competition, because many people or companies are trying to win the same thing.
entries.usage: Very common for markets, industries, admissions, jobs and sports: *a highly competitive market / field / program*. It usually describes the situation rather than a person's character; *fiercely competitive* is stronger and suggests rivals fighting hard. With pay, *a highly competitive salary* has a different sense: pay that compares very well with other employers.
entries.pattern: a highly competitive + market / field / industry / program
examples: Getting into nursing school here is **highly competitive**; only about one in five applicants is accepted.
The smartphone market is **highly competitive**, so prices drop quickly after each new launch.
My daughter plays in a **highly competitive** soccer league, and some of the parents take it way too seriously.

drill.sentence: The art residency is free, but the selection process is {{highly competitive}}: hundreds of people apply for six spots.
drill.hint: very hard to win because so many people want the same thing (adverb: not *very*, *extremely* or *fiercely*)

entries.related: *fiercely competitive* — stronger, rivals fighting hard; *cutthroat* — informal and critical, competition with no mercy; *a crowded market* — many companies selling the same thing.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: In a way that damages or loses something else, as the price for getting what you want.
entries.usage: Usually critical of a bad trade-off: *speed at the expense of quality*, *profits at the expense of safety*. It takes a noun or *-ing* form after *of*. With people, the possessive form means that person pays or is made to look silly: *a joke at my expense*.
entries.pattern: A at the expense of B / at someone's expense
examples: He built a successful career, but **at the expense of** his health and his marriage.
The new mall brought jobs to the area, but **at the expense of** the last open field in town.
Budget airlines keep fares low **at the expense of** legroom and comfort.

drill.sentence: Some parents push their kids to get perfect grades {{at the expense of}} sleep and friendships.
drill.hint: while sacrificing (not *at the cost of*)

mistake.wrong: He got rich on the expense of his workers.
mistake.right: He got rich at the expense of his workers.
mistake.why: The fixed phrase uses *at*; German *auf Kosten* and similar phrases in other languages lead learners to say *on*.

entries.related: *at the cost of* — very close, often for a heavy price; *at someone's expense* — that person pays or is laughed at; *in exchange for* — a neutral trade, no harm implied.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Pay that is as good as, or better than, what similar employers offer for the same kind of job.
entries.usage: A standard phrase in job ads and recruiting emails: *We offer a competitive salary and benefits.* Because it gives no number, many job seekers find it vague and ask for the actual range. *Competitive pay* and *a competitive benefits package* are common variants.
entries.pattern: offer / pay (someone) a competitive salary (and benefits)
examples: The hospital is struggling to hire nurses even though it offers **a competitive salary** and a signing bonus.
The ad promised **a competitive salary**, but it didn't mention a single number.
If the district wants to keep good teachers, it has to pay **a competitive salary**.

drill.sentence: Small nonprofits often can't offer {{a competitive salary}}, so they attract staff with flexible hours instead.
drill.hint: pay that keeps up with what similar employers offer (not *good* or *decent*)

entries.related: *competitive pay* — the same; *a generous salary* — clearly high; *a decent salary* — good enough, more informal.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To pay money, especially an amount that is due, such as a bill, rent or one part of a loan.
entries.usage: Common with banks, landlords, utilities and customer service: *make a payment on your loan / card*, *make a payment to someone*, *make your monthly payments*. It is more formal than plain *pay*, which people use more in casual talk. The usual negatives are *miss a payment* and *fall behind on payments*.
entries.pattern: make a payment (on + loan / card) / make a payment to + someone
examples: You can **make a payment** online, by phone or at any of our branches.
We finally **made the last payment** on our mortgage and celebrated with a big dinner.
If you can't **make a payment** this month, call the lender before the due date.

drill.sentence: My credit card bill is due Friday, so I need to {{make a payment}} before then.
drill.hint: send the money that is owed (three words, not *pay it*)

mistake.why: *Payment* goes with *make*, not *do*; you can also just say *I paid*.

entries.related: *pay* — the plain verb; *pay off* — pay all of a debt; *miss a payment* — fail to pay on time.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Something that lets a company, product or person do better than rivals, such as lower costs, a better location or a strong brand.
entries.usage: A core business term in strategy talk, reports and news: *give someone a competitive advantage*, *gain / have / lose a competitive advantage over rivals*. Outside business it also describes athletes and job seekers. *A competitive edge* means the same and sounds a little more informal.
entries.pattern: give someone / gain / have a competitive advantage (over + rivals)
examples: Their **competitive advantage** is simple: same-day delivery in every major city.
Speaking Spanish gave her **a competitive advantage** when she applied for jobs in Miami.
Training at high altitude can give long-distance runners **a competitive advantage**.

drill.sentence: Being open until midnight gives the little pharmacy {{a competitive advantage}} over the big chains.
drill.hint: something that helps it beat its rivals (adjective + noun, not *an edge*)

entries.related: *a competitive edge* — the same, more informal; *an unfair advantage* — critical; *a selling point* — a feature that attracts buyers.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To give money or goods to a charity, cause or organization without expecting anything back.
entries.usage: Common in fundraising emails, on websites and in speech: *make a donation to + organization*, *make a donation in someone's name / in memory of someone*. It is a little more formal than the verb *donate*, which most people use in conversation. *Give a donation* exists but is much less common.
entries.pattern: make a donation to + organization (in memory of + someone)
examples: Instead of sending flowers, the family asked guests to **make a donation** to the local animal shelter.
You can **make a donation** at the register when you pay for your groceries.
Every December, my parents **make a donation** to the food bank in their grandchildren's names.

drill.sentence: After the tornado, thousands of people went online to {{make a donation}} to the Red Cross.
drill.hint: give money to help victims (verb + noun, not *send money*)

entries.related: *donate* — the one-word verb; *contribute* — formal, money or effort; *pledge* — promise to give later.

entries.label: adverb + participle
entries.meaning: Respected and admired by many people, especially by experts or others in the same field.
entries.usage: Used for people, institutions and work: *a highly regarded surgeon / school / novel*. Typical patterns are *be highly regarded as + role* and *be highly regarded for + quality*. American style guides do not put a hyphen after an *-ly* adverb, so write *a highly regarded chef*.
entries.pattern: a highly regarded + person / place / be highly regarded (as / for + noun)
examples: She's a **highly regarded** heart surgeon, and patients travel from other states to see her.
The restaurant is **highly regarded** for its seafood, so make a reservation well in advance.
He left a **highly regarded** law firm to open a small practice in his hometown.

drill.sentence: My uncle never went to college, but he's {{highly regarded}} as one of the best carpenters in the county.
drill.hint: admired by many people (the adverb is not *well*; the participle is not *respected* or *thought of*)

entries.related: *highly respected* — almost the same; *well regarded* — a little weaker; *highly thought of* — more conversational.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To earn more money from something than you spend on it.
entries.usage: The everyday verb is *make*: *make a profit on / from something*, *make a small / quick / huge profit*. Business news also uses *turn a profit*, often for the first profit after losses. For the opposite, Americans usually say *lose money* or *take a loss*; *make a loss* sounds British.
entries.pattern: make a (small / quick / huge) profit on / from + noun
examples: The bakery didn't **make a profit** until its third year.
We bought the house cheap, fixed it up and **made a profit** of about forty thousand dollars.
The airline expects to **make a profit** this year for the first time since the pandemic.

drill.sentence: The kids sold lemonade all afternoon, but after buying cups and lemons they barely {{made a profit}}.
drill.hint: earned more than they spent (the noun is not *money*)

mistake.wrong: The store made a benefit last year.
mistake.right: The store made a profit last year.
mistake.why: French *bénéfice* and Spanish *beneficio* mean profit, but English *benefit* means an advantage, not money earned.

entries.related: *turn a profit* — become profitable, often for the first time; *break even* — earn exactly what you spent; *lose money* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A first, unfinished version of a piece of writing, which you expect to change a lot.
entries.usage: Common at school, at work and in creative writing: *write / send someone a rough draft (of something)*. Saying *It's just a rough draft* warns readers not to judge the details yet. *First draft* only says it is the first version; *rough* stresses that it is messy and unpolished.
entries.pattern: write / send someone a rough draft (of + text)
examples: I have **a rough draft** of my wedding toast, but it's still way too long.
Students must turn in **a rough draft** by Friday and the final essay two weeks later.
Here's **a rough draft** of my email to the school. Does it sound too angry?

drill.sentence: Don't worry about spelling yet; just get {{a rough draft}} down on paper and fix it later.
drill.hint: an unpolished early version (the adjective is not *first*)

entries.related: *first draft* — the first version, not necessarily messy; *final draft* — the finished version; *outline* — a list of main points, not full text.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Physically fit and healthy, or, about things and situations, in good condition and working well.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation for people (*She's in really good shape for her age*), things (*The car's in good shape*) and situations (*The budget is in good shape*). There is no article before the adjective, and *in great / excellent / bad shape* follow the same pattern. *Get in shape* means to become fit by exercising.
entries.pattern: be / stay in good shape (for + age)
examples: My grandfather walks three miles every morning and is **in good shape** for eighty-five.
The house is old, but the roof and the plumbing are **in good shape**.
After a rough first year, the company is finally back **in good shape** financially.

drill.sentence: The used bike was cheap, and the tires and brakes were still {{in good shape}}.
drill.hint: in fine condition (plain adjective, not *great*; the noun is not *condition*)

mistake.wrong: I'm in a good shape now that I run every day.
mistake.right: I'm in good shape now that I run every day.
mistake.why: The phrase has no article: *in good shape*, *in great shape*.

entries.related: *in shape* — fit; *out of shape* — unfit; *in good condition* — for things, not for people's fitness.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To become as good, skilled or successful as you are capable of being.
entries.usage: Common in education, coaching, HR and self-help language, so it can sound a little like a slogan. The possessive changes with the subject (*reach her / their full potential*), and it often appears in hopeful or regretful frames: *help kids reach their full potential*, *never reached his full potential*. *Fulfill* and *realize your potential* are slightly more formal.
entries.pattern: reach (my / her / their) full potential / help someone reach their full potential
examples: Good coaching helped her **reach her full potential** as a swimmer.
Injuries meant he never **reached his full potential** in the NBA.
The program gives kids from low-income families the support they need to **reach their full potential**.

drill.sentence: With better teachers and smaller classes, many of these students could {{reach their full potential}}.
drill.hint: become as good as they can possibly be (verb: not *realize*, *fulfill* or *achieve*)

entries.related: *realize / fulfill your potential* — slightly more formal; *live up to your potential* — do as well as people expect; *untapped potential* — ability not yet used.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A mix of positive and negative opinions from critics or users about a movie, book, product or performance.
entries.usage: Standard in arts and product journalism: *get / receive / open to mixed reviews*. It suggests the result was neither a hit nor a flop. Do not confuse it with *mixed feelings*, which are your own uncertain emotions about something.
entries.pattern: get / receive / open to mixed reviews (from + critics)
examples: The movie got **mixed reviews**: critics loved the acting but hated the ending.
The new phone has received **mixed reviews**, mostly because of its battery life.
The restaurant opened to **mixed reviews**, but now it's packed every weekend.

drill.sentence: The new season of the show has gotten {{mixed reviews}}; some fans love it and others say it's boring.
drill.hint: some positive and some negative opinions from critics (not *reactions* or *feedback*)

entries.related: *rave reviews* — very positive; *scathing reviews* — very negative; *a mixed reception* — the general reaction, not only from critics.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Working very well and producing the result that was intended.
entries.usage: Common in health, education, business and marketing writing: *a highly effective treatment / method / strategy*. It is often followed by *at* or *in* + *-ing*, or by *against* for medicines and products: *highly effective against ticks*. In casual speech people more often say *works really well*.
entries.pattern: highly effective (at / in + -ing / against + noun)
examples: The new traffic lights have been **highly effective** at reducing accidents near the school.
She's a quiet but **highly effective** manager who gets the best out of people.
Ice, rest and a little patience are **highly effective** for most minor sprains.

drill.sentence: This cheap spray turned out to be {{highly effective}} against the ants in our kitchen.
drill.hint: worked very well (adverb + adjective, not *very* or *extremely*)

entries.related: *very effective* — plainer; *remarkably effective* — surprisingly so; *efficient* — gets the result without wasting time or money.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To have all the qualities, qualifications or conditions that are needed for something.
entries.usage: Common in applications, admissions, building codes and official rules: *meet the requirements for + noun*, *meet all / the minimum requirements*. *Meet* is the standard verb; *fulfill* and *satisfy the requirements* are more formal, and *fulfill* is often about completing tasks (*fulfill the degree requirements*).
entries.pattern: meet the (minimum / basic) requirements for + noun
examples: Unfortunately, your application does not **meet the requirements** for this position.
Our old apartment didn't **meet the requirements** of the city's new fire code.
Before you fly, check that your carry-on bag **meets the requirements** for size and weight.

drill.sentence: Sorry, but your passport photo doesn't {{meet the requirements}}: the background has to be white.
drill.hint: have the qualities that are needed (verb: not *fulfill* or *satisfy*)

entries.related: *fulfill / satisfy the requirements* — more formal; *qualify for* — meet the conditions to get something; *fall short of* — not quite meet.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A friendly, kind reception that makes someone feel happy to have arrived.
entries.usage: Common in speeches, emails, travel and event language: *give / receive / get a warm welcome*, and formally *extend a warm welcome to someone*. *Please give a warm welcome to …* is the standard way to introduce a speaker. The opposite is *a cold* or *frosty reception*.
entries.pattern: give someone / receive / get a warm welcome (from + people)
examples: When we arrived in the village, the whole family came out to give us **a warm welcome**.
Ladies and gentlemen, please give **a warm welcome** to tonight's speaker, Dr. Lena Ortiz.
New employees always get **a warm welcome** and a free lunch on their first day.

drill.sentence: The team came home from the tournament without a trophy, but fans at the airport still gave them {{a warm welcome}}.
drill.hint: a friendly reception (the adjective describes temperature)

entries.related: *a hero's welcome* — a celebration for someone returning; *a cold / frosty reception* — unfriendly; *make someone feel welcome* — be friendly to a newcomer.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To provide what someone needs or requires.
entries.usage: Common in business, healthcare, social services and marketing: *meet the needs of + group*, *meet customers' needs*, *meet your needs*. *Meet* is the usual verb; *fulfill* or *satisfy* needs are more formal. The same verb goes with *demand* and *expectations*: *meet demand*, *meet expectations*.
entries.pattern: meet someone's needs / meet the needs of + group
examples: The school hired two more aides to **meet the needs** of students with disabilities.
We switched to a bigger phone plan because the old one didn't **meet our needs** anymore.
A good bank should **meet your needs**, not push products you don't want.

drill.sentence: The town's tiny clinic can't {{meet the needs}} of a population that has doubled in ten years.
drill.hint: provide what is required by (verb: not *serve* or *address*)

entries.related: *cater to* — provide what a group wants; *serve the needs of* — similar, more formal; *meet demand* — supply enough.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Permanently; for all future time, with no plan to change back or return.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and news, usually at the end of the clause: *leave / move / quit / close for good*. It sounds natural and a little emotional; *permanently* is the neutral, more formal word. It has nothing to do with being good, so do not confuse it with *for the good of*.
entries.pattern: leave / move / quit / close + for good
examples: After ten years in Chicago, they moved back to Texas **for good**.
The diner on Main Street is closing **for good** at the end of the month.
I think I've finally quit smoking **for good** this time.

drill.sentence: She says she's leaving the band {{for good}} this time, not just taking a break.
drill.hint: permanently (two words, not *forever*)

entries.related: *permanently* — more formal; *forever* — similar, more emotional; *once and for all* — finally and completely, often about ending a problem.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A chance to begin again, often in a new place, job or relationship, after problems or failure.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and stories about moving, divorce, recovery or debt: *want / need / get a fresh start*, *make a fresh start in + place*. It sounds hopeful. *Start over* and *start from scratch* are related verbs.
entries.pattern: make / get / need a fresh start (in + place)
examples: After the divorce, she moved to Denver for **a fresh start**.
January feels like **a fresh start**, so that's when a lot of people join a gym.
The new owners promised workers **a fresh start** after years of bad management.

drill.sentence: He paid off all his debts and felt like he finally had {{a fresh start}}.
drill.hint: a chance to begin again (not *a clean slate* or *a new beginning*)

entries.related: *a clean slate* — a past record that no longer counts; *start over* — begin again; *turn over a new leaf* — change your behavior for the better.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To fail to finish or submit something by the time it is due.
entries.usage: Very common at work, at school and with official forms: *miss a / the deadline (for + task)*. The opposite is *meet a deadline*, and *make the deadline* is a casual variant. When the deadline is the subject, say *the deadline passed*.
entries.pattern: miss a / the deadline (for + task)
examples: If you **miss the deadline**, you'll have to pay a late fee.
We **missed the deadline** for summer camp registration, so the kids are home all July.
The contractor has **missed every deadline** so far, and our kitchen still has no cabinets.

drill.sentence: I stayed up until 3 a.m. because I couldn't afford to {{miss the deadline}} for my scholarship application.
drill.hint: fail to submit on time (the opposite of *meet* it)

mistake.wrong: I lost the deadline because I was sick.
mistake.right: I missed the deadline because I was sick.
mistake.why: Spanish and Portuguese use one verb (*perder*) for *lose* and *miss*, but in English you *miss* a deadline.

entries.related: *meet a deadline* — finish on time; *a tight deadline* — little time; *extend a deadline* — give more time.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Having a high level of formal education, usually a university degree or more.
entries.usage: Common in news, social research and descriptions of people or workforces: *a highly educated workforce / population*. It is about schooling, not manners. *Well educated* is similar and slightly broader, often including general knowledge.
entries.pattern: a highly educated + workforce / population / person
examples: Boston has a **highly educated** workforce, thanks partly to its many universities.
Both of her parents are **highly educated**, but they couldn't find jobs in their fields at first.
Even **highly educated** people fall for online scams.

drill.sentence: The little beach town is full of {{highly educated}} retirees: former professors, doctors and engineers.
drill.hint: with a lot of formal schooling (adverb + adjective, not *well*)

mistake.wrong: Her children are very educated; they always say please and thank you.
mistake.right: Her children are very polite; they always say please and thank you.
mistake.why: *Educated* is about schooling; for good manners use *polite* or *well-mannered*, unlike Spanish *educado* or Italian *educato*.

entries.related: *well educated* — similar, often includes general knowledge; *well read* — has read a lot; *overqualified* — has more education than a job needs.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To behave in a way that other people, especially younger or junior ones, can copy.
entries.usage: Common in parenting, teaching, sports and leadership talk: *set a good / bad example for + people*. American English usually uses *for*; British English often uses *to*. *Lead by example* is a related phrase.
entries.pattern: set a good / bad example for + someone
examples: Put your phone away at dinner; you're supposed to **set an example for** the kids.
The captain **set an example for** the whole team by showing up first to every practice.
When the CEO took a pay cut, she **set an example for** other executives in the industry.

drill.sentence: As the oldest of five, I always felt I had to {{set a good example for}} my younger brothers and sisters.
drill.hint: behave in a way they could copy (not *be a role model for*)

mistake.wrong: Teachers should give a good example to their students.
mistake.right: Teachers should set a good example for their students.
mistake.why: The verb is *set*; *give an example* means to name one case to explain something.

entries.related: *lead by example* — show others by doing it yourself; *be a role model* — be someone people admire and copy; *give an example* — name one case to explain something.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Something useful you learn from an experience, often from a mistake or a hard situation.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, stories and interviews: *learn a valuable lesson (about + noun)*, *teach someone a valuable lesson*. It is often a positive way to talk about a failure: *It was a valuable lesson.* *A hard* or *painful lesson* stresses that learning it hurt.
entries.pattern: learn / teach someone a valuable lesson (about + noun)
examples: Losing my wallet in Rome taught me **a valuable lesson** about keeping my cards in different places.
The team lost badly, but the coach called it **a valuable lesson** for a young squad.
Our first product flopped, and it was **a valuable lesson** in listening to customers.

drill.sentence: Running out of gas in the desert taught us {{a valuable lesson}}: always fill up when you can.
drill.hint: something useful we learned (adjective: not *hard* or *important*)

entries.related: *a hard / painful lesson* — learned through suffering; *learn your lesson* — learn not to repeat a mistake; *a wake-up call* — an event that shows you a problem.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To own or manage a company or shop and be responsible for how it operates every day.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing: *run a (small / family / successful) business*. *Run* is the normal verb for managing any organization: *run a restaurant, a school, a department*. *Own a business* only says it belongs to you; *run* says you manage it.
entries.pattern: run a (small / family) business / run a + restaurant / shop / school
examples: My aunt has **run a business** out of her garage for twenty years, fixing lawnmowers.
**Running a business** means you never really take a day off.
You don't need an MBA to **run a successful business**, but you do need to understand cash flow.

drill.sentence: My grandparents {{ran a business}} selling furniture in Ohio for almost forty years.
drill.hint: managed a company (verb: not *owned* or *had*)

mistake.wrong: My parents lead a small bakery.
mistake.right: My parents run a small bakery.
mistake.why: German *führen* tempts learners to say *lead*; for a store or small company, natives say *run*, while *lead* is for people, teams and large organizations.

entries.related: *start / launch a business* — begin one; *own a business* — have it, maybe without managing it; *manage* — more formal, often someone else's company.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Very close to doing, reaching or experiencing something, often something important.
entries.usage: Common in speech and news, with a noun or *-ing* form: *on the verge of tears / bankruptcy*, *on the verge of quitting*. It can be good or bad: *on the verge of a breakthrough*. *On the brink of* is similar but usually about danger or disaster.
entries.pattern: on the verge of + noun / -ing
examples: She was **on the verge of** tears when they told her the flight was canceled.
The little bookstore was **on the verge of** closing until the neighborhood raised money to save it.
Scientists say they are **on the verge of** a cheap blood test for the disease.

drill.sentence: I was {{on the verge of}} giving up on the puzzle when I finally found the missing piece.
drill.hint: about to, but not yet (not *on the brink of* or *close to*)

mistake.wrong: The company is on the verge to close.
mistake.right: The company is on the verge of closing.
mistake.why: *On the verge* takes *of* + noun or *-ing*, never a *to* infinitive.

entries.related: *on the brink of* — similar, usually before something bad; *about to* + verb — will happen very soon; *close to* + noun / *-ing* — plainer.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To try to get elected to a public position, such as mayor, school board member or member of Congress.
entries.usage: The standard American phrase in news and conversation. *Run for* can also take the position directly, with no article before a single office: *run for mayor*, *run for city council*. British English usually says *stand for* (*stand for Parliament*), so Americans hear *stand* as British.
entries.pattern: run for office / run for + mayor / Congress / city council
examples: After twenty years as a teacher, she decided to **run for office** and won a seat on the school board.
In a small town, it's easier than you'd think to **run for office**.
He was a popular sheriff, and people kept urging him to **run for office** at the state level.

drill.sentence: Our local librarian surprised everyone when she announced she would {{run for office}} next year.
drill.hint: try to get elected (the general phrase, not a specific job like *mayor*)

entries.related: *stand for election* — British; *campaign* — work to win votes; *hold office* — be in the position.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Completely necessary; something you cannot do without.
entries.usage: Common in speech, instructions and persuasive writing: *it's absolutely essential to + verb / that …*, *absolutely essential for + noun*. *Essential* already means *necessary*, so it goes with *absolutely* or *really*; *very essential* sounds wrong to most natives. In ads (*ten absolutely essential gadgets*) it can sound like hype.
entries.pattern: it's absolutely essential to + verb / that … / absolutely essential for + noun
examples: A good pair of hiking boots is **absolutely essential** on this trail; it's all loose rock.
It's **absolutely essential** that you bring your passport, or they won't let you board.
For new parents, a few hours of sleep isn't a luxury; it's **absolutely essential**.

drill.sentence: When you're kayaking in cold water, a life jacket is {{absolutely essential}}.
drill.hint: completely necessary (adverb: not *really*; adjective: not *vital*, *crucial* or *necessary*)

mistake.wrong: Sunscreen is very essential at the beach.
mistake.right: Sunscreen is absolutely essential at the beach.
mistake.why: *Essential* already means *completely necessary*, so it takes *absolutely* or *really*, not *very*.

entries.related: *absolutely vital / crucial* — similar; *indispensable* — formal; *nice to have* — useful but not necessary.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A person or thing with a good chance of being chosen for a job, award, position or role.
entries.usage: Common in hiring, elections, awards and sports: *a strong candidate for + job / prize*. It also describes things and places: *a strong candidate for the new stadium site*. The opposite is *a weak candidate*; *the front-runner* is the one most likely to win.
entries.pattern: a strong candidate for + job / award / role
examples: With ten years of experience and great references, she's **a strong candidate** for the job.
His performance in the war drama makes him **a strong candidate** for an Oscar this year.
The old warehouse by the river is **a strong candidate** for the new community center.

drill.sentence: Our neighborhood is {{a strong candidate}} for the new subway stop, but the city hasn't decided yet.
drill.hint: an option with a good chance of being chosen (adjective: not *good*, *top* or *leading*; the noun is not *contender*)

entries.related: *the front-runner* — the one most likely to win; *a shoo-in* — informal, certain to win; *a long shot* — unlikely to be chosen.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To have a body temperature that is higher than normal because you are sick.
entries.usage: Very common in American conversation, especially about children: *be running a fever*, *run a high / low-grade fever*. *Have a fever* means the same. British speakers more often say *have* or *run a temperature*, and Americans give the number in Fahrenheit (normal is about 98.6).
entries.pattern: be running a (high / low-grade) fever / run a fever of + number
examples: Jake's **running a fever**, so I'm keeping him home from school today.
If you're **running a fever**, please work from home instead of coming to the office.
She **ran a fever** for three days after the trip, so her doctor ordered some tests.

drill.sentence: The baby was {{running a fever}} all night, so we called the pediatrician first thing in the morning.
drill.hint: had a higher body heat than normal (verb + noun; the noun is not *temperature*)

mistake.wrong: My son has fever, so he can't come to the party.
mistake.right: My son has a fever, so he can't come to the party.
mistake.why: German *Fieber haben* has no article, but in English *fever* takes *a*: *have a fever*, *run a fever*.

entries.related: *have a fever* — the same, more neutral; *have a temperature* — British; *feel feverish* — feel hot and sick, maybe without measuring.

entries.term: be in the mood for something
entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To feel like doing or having something at a particular moment.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation: *be in the mood for + noun / -ing*, *be in the mood to + verb*. It is often negative: *I'm not in the mood for jokes*, and *I'm not in the mood* alone means you are tired or annoyed. *Feel like* + noun / *-ing* means the same.
entries.pattern: be (not) in the mood for + noun / -ing / to + verb
examples: I'm not really **in the mood for** pizza tonight. How about Thai?
After a long week, nobody was **in the mood for** a two-hour meeting.
Are you **in the mood for** a movie, or should we just go to bed early?

drill.sentence: The sun's finally out, and I'm totally {{in the mood for}} a long bike ride along the river.
drill.hint: feeling like having (not *up for*)

mistake.wrong: I have no lust for a party tonight.
mistake.right: I'm not in the mood for a party tonight.
mistake.why: German *Lust* is not English *lust*, which means strong sexual desire; use *be in the mood for* or *feel like*.

entries.related: *feel like* + noun / *-ing* — the same; *be up for* — be willing, informal; *in a bad mood* — irritated.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A process that takes a long time, often longer than people would like.
entries.usage: Common in official, legal, medical and business contexts: *It's a lengthy process*, *go through a lengthy approval process*. *Lengthy* is more formal than *long* and often hints at a complaint about delay. Typical verbs are *go through*, *begin* and *involve*.
entries.pattern: be / go through a lengthy (approval / application) process
examples: Getting a building permit in this city is **a lengthy process**, so start early.
Adopting a child is **a lengthy process** that can take two years or more.
Recovering from knee surgery is **a lengthy process**, but most people get back to running eventually.

drill.sentence: Fixing a mistake on your credit report can be {{a lengthy process}}, so keep copies of every letter.
drill.hint: something that takes a long time (adjective: not *long*, *slow* or *time-consuming*)

entries.related: *a long, drawn-out process* — critical, slow and tiring; *time-consuming* — takes a lot of time; *a quick fix* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To receive an increase in your regular pay from your employer.
entries.usage: The everyday American phrase; British English says *get a pay rise*. Common forms are *ask for a raise*, *give someone a raise* and *get a four percent raise*. HR documents use the more formal *salary increase*.
entries.pattern: get / ask for / give someone a raise (of + amount)
examples: She finally **got a raise** after two years, so we went out to celebrate.
Most workers at the plant **got a raise** of about four percent this year.
If I don't **get a raise** soon, I'm going to start looking for another job.

drill.sentence: My boss said I'd {{get a raise}} if I took on the two new accounts.
drill.hint: be paid more every month from now on (not a *promotion* or a one-time *bonus*)

entries.related: *a pay rise* — British; *a promotion* — a higher position, usually with more pay; *a bonus* — a one-time extra payment.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Completely acceptable or in good condition, with nothing wrong.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation to reassure someone or to defend something: *It's perfectly fine*, *a perfectly fine car*. With strong stress on *perfectly*, it can sound defensive or annoyed: *I'm perfectly fine, thank you.* It can also mean *acceptable but nothing special*: *The food was perfectly fine.*
entries.pattern: be perfectly fine / a perfectly fine + noun
examples: Don't worry about the stain; the shirt is **perfectly fine**.
There's no need to buy a new laptop. Your old one is **perfectly fine** for email and browsing.
The hotel was **perfectly fine**, but I wouldn't stay there again for that price.

drill.sentence: You don't need to call a mechanic; that noise is normal and your car is {{perfectly fine}}.
drill.hint: with nothing wrong at all (adverb: not *just*, *totally*, *completely* or *absolutely*)

entries.related: *totally fine* — more casual; *just fine* — acceptable, sometimes a little defensive; *perfectly good* — still usable, nothing wrong with it.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To complete a task successfully, often without worrying about style or perfection.
entries.usage: Informal and very common at work, in sports and about tools: *This old drill gets the job done.* It praises practical results over elegance or method. Typical frames are *whatever it takes to get the job done* and *someone who gets the job done*.
entries.pattern: get the job done / something gets the job done
examples: It's not the prettiest solution, but it **gets the job done**.
Our goalie isn't flashy, but she **gets the job done** every single game.
A cheap pair of pliers will **get the job done** if you only need them once.

drill.sentence: I don't care how you fix the sink, as long as you {{get the job done}} before my parents arrive.
drill.hint: finish the task successfully (four words, not *get it done*)

entries.related: *get it done* — the same, shorter; *do the trick* — work well enough to solve a problem; *cut corners* — finish quickly by skipping steps.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: An uncomfortable moment when nobody speaks, usually because someone said something embarrassing or nobody knows what to say.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and storytelling: *there was an awkward silence*, *fill / break an awkward silence*, *an awkward silence fell*. *A long pause* is neutral; *dead silence* is complete silence, often from shock.
entries.pattern: there was an awkward silence / fill / break an awkward silence
examples: When he asked how her husband was, there was **an awkward silence**; they had separated a month earlier.
On first dates, I ask lots of questions to avoid **an awkward silence**.
Nobody laughed at the boss's joke, and **an awkward silence** filled the room.

drill.sentence: When Dad asked my brother about his grades at dinner, {{an awkward silence}} fell over the table.
drill.hint: a moment when nobody talked and everyone felt uneasy (adjective: not *uncomfortable*)

entries.related: *an uncomfortable silence* — similar; *a pregnant pause* — a pause full of meaning; *break the ice* — make strangers feel relaxed.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To take someone somewhere in your car, usually as a favor.
entries.usage: The everyday American phrase: *give someone a ride to + place / home*. British English says *give someone a lift*. *Can you give me a ride?* is the standard request; *pick someone up* describes only the start of the trip.
entries.pattern: give someone a ride (to + place / home)
examples: My car's in the shop. Could you **give me a ride** to work tomorrow?
My sister's friend **gave her a ride** home after soccer practice.
Don't walk home in this rain; I'll **give you a ride**.

drill.sentence: Thanks for {{giving me a ride}}; I'd never have made it to the interview on time.
drill.hint: taking me in your car (the noun is not *lift*)

entries.related: *give someone a lift* — British; *drive someone* — the same idea as a verb; *carpool* — share car trips regularly.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A lack of confidence in your own value, so that you often feel you are not good enough.
entries.usage: Common in psychology, health and everyday talk: *have / suffer from / struggle with low self-esteem*. The opposite is *high self-esteem*. *Self-confidence* is about trusting your abilities; *self-esteem* is about your basic sense of worth.
entries.pattern: have / suffer from / struggle with low self-esteem
examples: Years of being bullied at school left him with **low self-esteem**.
Teenagers with **low self-esteem** are often very sensitive to comments online.
She struggled with **low self-esteem** until she joined a running club and started setting goals.

drill.sentence: Kids who are constantly criticized at home often grow up with {{low self-esteem}}.
drill.hint: a poor sense of their own worth (not *insecurity*; the noun is not *confidence*)

mistake.why: *Self-esteem* is uncountable, so it takes no *a*.

entries.related: *insecurity* — feeling unsure of yourself; *self-confidence* — trust in your abilities; *a bruised ego* — hurt pride after a failure.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Said unofficially, on the understanding that it will not be published or repeated with your name.
entries.usage: From journalism, where a source speaks *off the record* to a reporter; now also common at work and in daily life to mark something confidential. Typical forms are *speak / talk off the record* and *Off the record, …* at the start of a sentence. The opposite is *on the record*.
entries.pattern: speak / talk off the record / Off the record, …
examples: One airport official agreed to talk **off the record** about the delays.
**Off the record**, I don't think the new manager will last a year.
My friend at the bank told me, **off the record**, that our branch is closing next year.

drill.sentence: I'll tell you what really happened, but this is strictly {{off the record}}, so don't quote me.
drill.hint: not for publication (three words, not *confidential*)

entries.related: *on the record* — official, can be quoted; *between you and me* — private, casual; *confidential* — formal, to be kept secret.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To tell your employer that you are leaving your job two weeks before your last day.
entries.usage: The standard American custom; in most US jobs it is a courtesy, not a legal requirement. Typical forms are *give (my) two weeks' notice*, *put in my two weeks' notice* and, casually, *put in my two weeks*. Note the apostrophe in *weeks'*.
entries.pattern: give / put in (your) two weeks' notice
examples: She found a better job and **gave two weeks' notice** the next morning.
I'm planning to **give my two weeks' notice** on Monday, but I haven't told my manager yet.
Most restaurants expect servers to **give two weeks' notice** before they leave.

drill.sentence: Before you {{give two weeks' notice}}, make sure the new employer has confirmed your start date.
drill.hint: tell your boss you're quitting, half a month ahead (verb: not *put in*)

entries.related: *hand in your notice* — more British; *resign* — formal; *quit* — informal; *be let go* — lose your job.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: So bad or wrong that it must not be allowed or tolerated.
entries.usage: A strong complaint, used in customer service, management, official statements and parenting: *This is completely unacceptable.* *Totally unacceptable* sounds more emotional, and *simply unacceptable* is common in official statements. It usually judges behavior, service or conditions, not people.
entries.pattern: It's completely unacceptable (that … / for someone to + verb)
examples: Waiting three hours in the emergency room with a broken arm is **completely unacceptable**.
The principal told the boys that their behavior on the bus was **completely unacceptable**.
It's **completely unacceptable** for a landlord to enter your apartment without notice.

drill.sentence: Charging a fifty-dollar cancellation fee for a twenty-dollar haircut is {{completely unacceptable}}.
drill.hint: so bad it can't be allowed (adverb: not *totally*, *absolutely* or *simply*)

entries.related: *totally unacceptable* — more emotional; *out of line* — informal, about behavior; *inexcusable* — impossible to forgive.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A warning about a danger that turns out not to be real, or a worry that turns out to be unnecessary.
entries.usage: Used literally for fire and car alarms and very often figuratively, after a health scare or a rumor: *turn out to be a false alarm*, *just a false alarm*. In conversation it often reassures: *Don't worry, it was a false alarm.*
entries.pattern: be / turn out to be (just) a false alarm
examples: The building was evacuated, but it turned out to be **a false alarm** caused by burned toast.
I thought I'd lost my passport, but it was **a false alarm**; it was in my coat pocket.
After three **false alarms** this month, nobody in the dorm takes the fire bell seriously anymore.

drill.sentence: Police searched the mall after a report of a suspicious bag, but it was {{a false alarm}}.
drill.hint: a warning about a danger that wasn't real (not *a hoax*, which is deliberate)

entries.related: *a hoax* — a deliberate trick; *a scare* — a sudden fright, possibly real; *cry wolf* — keep giving false warnings.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To make someone believe something through your words or behavior, often something that is not true.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and polite complaints: *You gave me the impression that breakfast was included.* It is softer than saying someone lied, so it is useful for diplomatic criticism. *Get the impression that* is the listener's side; *be under the impression that* means believing something, usually wrongly.
entries.pattern: give someone the impression that … / give the impression of + noun / -ing
examples: His short answers **gave me the impression that** he didn't want to talk.
The ad **gave customers the impression that** the watch was waterproof, but it isn't.
I didn't mean to **give you the impression that** I was angry; I was just tired.

drill.sentence: The salesman {{gave us the impression that}} the price included delivery, but it didn't.
drill.hint: made us believe, perhaps wrongly, (not *led us to believe*)

mistake.wrong: He made the impression that he was bored.
mistake.right: He gave the impression that he was bored.
mistake.why: German *den Eindruck machen* tempts learners to use *make*, but with a *that* clause English uses *give*; *make an impression (on someone)* means to impress someone.

entries.related: *get the impression that* — the listener's view; *be under the impression that* — believe, usually wrongly; *make an impression on* — impress.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: The option that is clearly the best or most suitable, so that little discussion is needed.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, news and reviews: *the obvious choice for + role / purpose*, *the obvious choice to + verb*. It can be slightly critical when the obvious option is not taken: *The obvious choice would have been …* It usually takes *the*, because there is only one.
entries.pattern: the obvious choice (for + role / to + verb)
examples: When the team needed someone to handle first aid, Ana, a nurse, was **the obvious choice**.
With three kids and a dog, a minivan was **the obvious choice**.
Lisbon seemed like **the obvious choice** for our anniversary trip: cheap flights, great food and lots of sunshine.

drill.sentence: He's the funniest guy we know, so he was {{the obvious choice}} to give the best man's speech.
drill.hint: the option that clearly made the most sense (adjective: not *natural*, *logical*, *perfect* or *best*)

entries.related: *a no-brainer* — informal, a very easy decision; *the natural choice* — the one that fits best; *a safe choice* — low risk, maybe boring.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To make someone believe that something good will happen when it probably will not.
entries.usage: Common in medicine, relationships, hiring and news, usually as something to avoid: *I don't want to give you false hope.* It sounds caring but honest. *Raise false hopes* is a common variant, especially in the news.
entries.pattern: give someone false hope / not want to give someone false hope
examples: The doctor was careful not to **give the family false hope** about his recovery.
A few sunny hours on Saturday morning **gave us false hope** that the beach trip was back on.
The company kept saying a decision was coming soon, which only **gave me false hope**.

drill.sentence: Don't tell the kids the dog might come back; it'll only {{give them false hope}}.
drill.hint: make them expect a good outcome that won't happen (not *get their hopes up*)

entries.related: *get someone's hopes up* — informal, similar; *lead someone on* — make someone think you are romantically interested; *an empty promise* — a promise that will not be kept.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Written down, especially as an official record that you can show later.
entries.usage: Common with contracts, at work and in legal advice: *get it in writing*, *put something in writing*, *confirm / submit something in writing*. There is no article before *writing*. The contrast is *verbally*, *in person* or *over the phone*.
entries.pattern: get / put / confirm something in writing
examples: The landlord promised to fix the heater, so I asked him to put it **in writing**.
Never accept a job offer until you have it **in writing**.
All complaints must be submitted **in writing** within thirty days.

drill.sentence: He promised to pay me back, but next time I'll get it {{in writing}}.
drill.hint: recorded as a document you can show later (not *on paper*)

entries.related: *on paper* — written down, or in theory; *verbally* — spoken, not written; *in black and white* — clearly written down.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A brave action or decision that involves some risk and that others might not dare to take.
entries.usage: Common in business, sports, news and conversation, usually as praise mixed with some doubt: *That's a bold move.* Said with a smile, it can be ironic about a risky or silly choice. Typical frames are *make a bold move* and *it was a bold move to + verb*.
entries.pattern: make a bold move / it was a bold move to + verb
examples: Quitting a safe job to open a bakery was **a bold move**, but it paid off.
The coach made **a bold move** by benching his top scorer in the final.
Ordering the spiciest dish on your first visit? That's **a bold move**.

drill.sentence: Proposing to her on the big screen in front of the whole stadium was {{a bold move}}; luckily, she said yes.
drill.hint: a decision that took courage (adjective: not *risky*, *brave*, *big* or *gutsy*)

entries.related: *a gutsy move* — informal, brave; *a calculated risk* — a risk taken after careful thought; *play it safe* — the opposite.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Extremely and unpleasantly cold, especially about weather or wind.
entries.usage: Common in weather reports and descriptions: *a bitterly cold wind / night / morning*, *it's bitterly cold out*. In casual speech you also hear *bitter cold* without *-ly*, and *the bitter cold* is the noun phrase. *Bitterly* goes with *cold* and with painful feelings (*bitterly disappointed*), never with heat; for extreme heat say *scorching hot* or *boiling hot*.
entries.pattern: bitterly cold + wind / night / morning / it's bitterly cold
examples: It was **bitterly cold** in Minneapolis last night, with temperatures well below zero.
We waited for the parade in a **bitterly cold** wind, holding cups of hot chocolate.
Bring gloves; it gets **bitterly cold** on the lake after sunset.

drill.sentence: The marathon started on a {{bitterly cold}} morning, and many runners wore trash bags to stay warm.
drill.hint: extremely and painfully chilly (use the *-ly* adverb; not *freezing* or *brutally*)

entries.related: *freezing cold* — informal, very common; *biting cold* — sharp and stinging; *chilly* — only a little cold.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To make an official complaint to an organization, a company or an authority, usually through a formal process.
entries.usage: Common in customer service, workplaces, housing and law: *file a complaint with + organization*, *against + person*, *about + issue*. *File* makes it official and recorded, unlike *complain*, which can just mean grumbling. *Lodge a complaint* is a formal variant, more common in British English.
entries.pattern: file a complaint with + organization / against + person (about + issue)
examples: After the airline lost her luggage twice, she **filed a complaint** with the Department of Transportation.
Several tenants **filed a complaint** against the landlord about the broken elevator.
If a coworker harasses you, you have the right to **file a complaint** with HR.

drill.sentence: The neighbors {{filed a complaint}} with the city about the barking dogs next door.
drill.hint: officially reported their problem (the verb is not *made* or *lodged*)

entries.related: *complain* — the general verb; *lodge a complaint* — formal, more British; *file a report* — give official information, for example to the police.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: One of several causes that together help to produce a result, usually a bad one.
entries.usage: Common in news, medicine, accident reports and analysis: *a contributing factor in / to + noun*. It says that something played a part but was not the only cause, so it sounds careful and neutral. Compare *the main cause* and *a key factor*.
entries.pattern: a (major / key) contributing factor in / to + noun
examples: Police said speed was **a contributing factor** in the crash.
Doctors think poor sleep may be **a contributing factor**, but it isn't the main cause of her headaches.
The heat wave was one of several **contributing factors** behind last week's power outages.

drill.sentence: Higher rent was {{a contributing factor}} in our decision to move, but it wasn't the main reason.
drill.hint: one of several causes (adjective + noun; the adjective is not *major* or *key*)

entries.related: *a key factor* — an important cause; *the root cause* — the deepest, original cause; *play a part in* — help to cause something.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To start a legal case against a person or organization in a court.
entries.usage: Very common in American news and conversation: *file a lawsuit against + someone (over / for + issue)*. *Sue* is the shorter verb, and *bring a lawsuit* is more formal. The person who files is *the plaintiff*.
entries.pattern: file a lawsuit against + someone (over / for + issue)
examples: The family **filed a lawsuit** against the hospital, claiming the surgeon made a serious mistake.
Three neighbors **filed a lawsuit** over the noise and smell from the new factory.
My cousin **filed a lawsuit** in small claims court to get back the eight hundred dollars a contractor owed her.

drill.sentence: After the gym refused to pay her medical bills, she {{filed a lawsuit}} against the owners.
drill.hint: started a court case (verb + noun; the verb is not *brought*; not *sued*)

entries.related: *sue* — the one-word verb; *settle (out of court)* — agree before a judgment; *press charges* — ask the police to accuse someone of a crime.

entries.label: participle + by + noun
entries.meaning: Something you must do because a law says so, not because you choose to.
entries.usage: Common on forms, signs and websites and in the news: *be required by law to + verb*, *as required by law*. It sounds official and neutral; in casual talk people say *it's the law*. *By law* alone can also start a sentence: *By law, employers must …*
entries.pattern: be required by law (to + verb) / as required by law
examples: In this state, drivers are **required by law** to stop for pedestrians in a crosswalk.
We collect your date of birth only because it's **required by law**.
Every bedroom in the new house has a smoke detector, as **required by law**.

drill.sentence: In New York City, restaurants are {{required by law}} to post their health inspection grade in the window.
drill.hint: forced by the legal system (participle + *by* + noun; not *mandatory*)

entries.related: *mandatory* — formal, required by a rule; *legally required* — the same, slightly more formal; *against the law* — illegal.
